title: Doe v. Great Expectations
summary: The dating service had to refund the customers’ payments because its contracts violated statutory requirements and it failed to disclose rights that would have affected their decisions to contract.
notes: The book distinguishes individual restitution, public civil penalties, and punitive damages. Statutory amounts and institutional descriptions here report the law applied in this 2005 opinion; they have not been checked as current legal advice.

sections.Parties: Two individual customers, identified as Doe and Roe, brought small-claims actions against a dating service in the New York City Civil Court. The court decided the similar matters together.
sections.Material Facts:
Doe paid $1,000 and Roe paid $3,790 for programs that principally made customer videos and profiles available for other customers to view. The printed agreements purported to promise zero social referrals and stated that the customer did not desire or expect referrals. Roe’s agreement also contained handwritten references to an enhanced marriage and shopper program, accompanied by assurances of introductions. Neither customer received the expected introductions.

The service maintained that it did not fall within the Dating Services Law because it merely provided a mechanism through which customers could contact one another. Its contracts omitted the required consumer bill of rights and nearly all mandated protections, although they included a three-day cooling-off cancellation notice. Among the omissions were specified referrals for higher-priced programs, refund rights, confidentiality, a right to place membership on hold, and return of personal materials.
sections.Procedural History: After hearing testimony in the two small-claims proceedings, the trial court awarded the full amounts paid, with interest. It also decided to send its decision to appropriate public enforcement officials because the form suggested a continuing pattern of violations. This is a trial-level application of the New York statute, not a general appellate rule about all dating services.
sections.Issue: Did the statute cover a service that facilitated matching without selecting matches itself, and what damages followed from its noncompliant agreements and disclosures?
sections.Holding: The statute applied. Each customer recovered the full payment as actual, restitutionary damages on the findings made in these cases.
sections.Reasoning:
The statutory definition covered supplying the means for social matching, including computer-based methods. The service could not avoid regulation by describing itself as providing no referrals while selling that kind of program. Under the statute as applied in the opinion, a contract without a specified minimum number of referrals could not charge more than $25. The excess payments therefore supplied a concrete measure of actual damages.

The remaining $25 required an additional explanation. Based on the customers’ testimony and their careful negotiations, the court found that they would not have signed contracts violating their rights if the required bill of rights had been provided. That supported refunding the balance as well. The court used the statute’s damages remedy rather than automatically declaring every noncomplying agreement void. Its separate reporting decision considered continuing public harm, the absence of a threat that might distort testimony, and prior litigation involving similar practices.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This case shows how legislation can impose terms and remedies that the printed agreement omits. It connects informed contracting, mandatory consumer protection, and recovery of payments.

topics.assent: The customers’ decisions to contract were affected by the failure to disclose mandatory rights.
topics.consumer-protection: A statutory definition and mandatory terms govern despite the business’s attempted description of its service.
topics.restitution: The court orders return of payments as actual damages under the statute.
topics.governing-law: Legislative requirements constrain what private forms can accomplish.
topics.adhesion: The same noncompliant printed terms were used across the customer agreements.

mnemonic.rationale: A dating service and its fees
